title: Distributive Conditional Types in TypeScript
summary: Understand distributive conditional types in TypeScript, see why unions and never behave unexpectedly, and use tuple wrappers to control distribution.
body_markdown:
A distributive conditional type is a conditional type whose checked type is a bare type parameter. When you pass a union to that parameter, TypeScript evaluates the conditional once for each member of the union and joins the results into a new union.


You write a small type-level check, pass it` string | number` , and expect` false` . TypeScript shows` boolean` . Or you pass` never` and get back` never` , which is neither branch you wrote.


This article skips the basics of` T extends U ? X : Y` ([Understanding infer in TypeScript](https://blog.openreplay.com/infer-typescript/) covers those). It goes straight to the distribution rule: how to turn it off, the` never` trap, and how to tell which behavior a given type has.


## Key Takeaways


- A conditional type distributes only when the type on the left of` extends` is a bare type parameter and the argument is a union.
- ` IsString<string | number>` resolves to` boolean` because TypeScript evaluates it as` IsString<string> | IsString<number>` .
- Writing` \[T\] extends \[U\]` , with both sides wrapped in a one-element tuple, turns distribution off.
- A distributive conditional type given` never` returns` never` , because` never` is the empty union and there are no members to evaluate.
- ` Exclude` and` Extract` are distributive. Since TypeScript 4.8,` NonNullable<T>` is defined as` T & {}` and is not a conditional type.


## Why Does a Union Check Return boolean Instead of false?


A distributive conditional type returns` boolean` for a mixed union because TypeScript checks each union member separately. The surprise comes from a plain-looking check:


```text
type   IsString<  T  >   =   T   extends   string   ?   true   :   false  ;


type   A   =   IsString  <  string   |   number  >;   // => boolean
```


Read as English, the question is whether` string | number` is a string. It isn’t, so most developers expect` false` . TypeScript answers a different question: it asks, for each member of the union, whether that member is a string.


## How Do Distributive Conditional Types Work?


A conditional type distributes when the type being checked, on the left of` extends` , is a bare[type parameter](https://blog.openreplay.com/generics-in-typescript/) and the argument for that parameter is a union. TypeScript evaluates the conditional once for each member and unions the results. The[TypeScript handbook describes this behavior](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html#distributive-conditional-types) using a` ToArray<string | number>` example, which resolves to` string\[\] | number\[\]` .


Applied to` IsString` , the expansion looks like this:


```text
type   A   =   IsString  <  string   |   number  >;
// = IsString<string> | IsString<number>
// = true | false
// = boolean
```


Two details follow from the rule. First, only the checked side distributes. The type on the right of` extends` is always compared as a single, whole type:


```text
type   HasString<  T  >   =   string   extends   T   ?   true   :   false  ;


type   B   =   HasString  <  string   |   number  >;   // => true
```


If the right side distributed, this would produce` boolean` . Second,` boolean` is the union` true | false` , so a distributive conditional type splits it into two checks just like any other union:


```text
type   Flip<  T  >   =   T   extends   true   ?   false   :   true  ;


type   C   =   Flip  <  boolean  >;   // => boolean (false | true)
```


## Built-In Utility Types That Rely on Distribution


` Exclude<T, U>` and` Extract<T, U>` are distributive conditional types. They walk a union one member at a time and keep the members that are not assignable to` U` (for` Exclude` ) or the members that are (for` Extract` ). The standard library defines them as` T extends U ? never : T` and` T extends U ? T : never` . Because a union absorbs` never` , the members that hit the` never` branch disappear from the result. The[Utility Types reference](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) lists both.


```text
type   D   =   Exclude  <  "  a  "   |   "  b  "   |   "  c  "  ,   "  a  "  >;                      // => "b" | "c"
type   E   =   Extract  <  string   |   number   |   (()   =>   void  ),   Function  >;   // => () => void
type   F   =   NonNullable  <  string   |   null   |   undefined  >;              // => string
```


` NonNullable` gives the result you would expect from a distributive filter, but it no longer is one.[Since TypeScript 4.8, NonNullable<T> is defined as T & {}](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-8.html) . It still removes` null` and` undefined` from a union, but it does so by intersection rather than by distributing a conditional type.


## Switching Distribution Off With` \[T\] extends \[U\]`


Writing` \[T\] extends \[U\]` , with both sides wrapped in a one-element tuple, turns distribution off, so TypeScript checks the union as one type. The handbook gives this bracket syntax as the way to avoid distribution:


```text
type   IsStringStrict<  T  >   =   [  T  ]   extends   [  string  ]   ?   true   :   false  ;


type   G1   =   IsString  <  string   |   number  >;         // => boolean
type   G2   =   IsStringStrict  <  string   |   number  >;   // => false
```


Any wrapper that leaves` T` no longer bare has the same effect, whether it is a tuple, a function type or an object type. The one-element tuple is the convention because it reads clearly and adds no other meaning. Wrap both sides.` \[T\] extends string` asks whether a tuple is a string, and the answer is always` false` .


## Why Does a Distributive Conditional Type Return` never` ?


A distributive conditional type given` never` returns` never` instead of either branch.` never` is the empty union, so there are no members to evaluate, and mapping over nothing produces the empty union. This is why a naive` IsNever` fails:


```text
type   IsNeverNaive<  T  >   =   T   extends   never   ?   true   :   false  ;


type   H1   =   IsNeverNaive  <  never  >;    // => never
type   H2   =   IsNeverNaive  <  string  >;   // => false
```


The fix is the same bracket opt-out.` \[never\]` is a real one-element tuple, so TypeScript runs the check:


```text
type   IsNever<  T  >   =   [  T  ]   extends   [  never  ]   ?   true   :   false  ;


type   I1   =   IsNever  <  never  >;    // => true
type   I2   =   IsNever  <  string  >;   // => false
```


## When Distribution Helps and When It Bites


Distribution helps when each union member needs its own result. A common case is mapping event names to handler types:


```text
interface   AppEvents   {
click  :   { x  :   number  ; y  :   number   };
keydown  :   { key  :   string   };
}


type   Handler<  E   extends   keyof   AppEvents  >   =
E   extends   keyof   AppEvents   ?   (  payload  :   AppEvents  [  E  ])   =>   void   :   never  ;


type   HandlerStrict<  E   extends   keyof   AppEvents  >   =
[  E  ]   extends   [  keyof   AppEvents  ]   ?   (  payload  :   AppEvents  [  E  ])   =>   void   :   never  ;


type   J1   =   Handler  <  "  click  "   |   "  keydown  "  >;
// => ((payload: { x: number; y: number; }) => void) | ((payload: { key: string; }) => void)


type   J2   =   HandlerStrict  <  "  click  "   |   "  keydown  "  >;
// => (payload: { x: number; y: number; } | { key: string; }) => void
```


` Handler` keeps each event paired with its own payload.` HandlerStrict` loses that pairing: it gives one function whose payload could be either shape, so a click handler type now admits` { key: string }` . A typed API layer usually wants the distributive version.


Distribution bites when the question concerns the whole union:


```text
type   AllStrings<  T  >   =   T   extends   string   ?   true   :   false  ;
type   AllStringsStrict<  T  >   =   [  T  ]   extends   [  string  ]   ?   true   :   false  ;


type   K1   =   AllStrings  <  "  a  "   |   1  >;         // => boolean
type   K2   =   AllStringsStrict  <  "  a  "   |   1  >;   // => false
```


In a form library, a check like` AllStrings` that is meant to reject a mixed field type returns` boolean` instead. Any downstream branch that tests the result against` true` or` false` then misbehaves. The bracketed form answers the question that was asked.


## How to Tell Which Behavior You Have


A conditional type distributes only if its type parameter appears unwrapped on the left of` extends` . If a conditional type returns an unexpected union, or returns` never` when you passed` never` , check that first.


Form Distributes?


` T extends …` Yes


` \[T\] extends \[…\]` No


` (string | number) extends string` No, because there is no type parameter


## Conclusion


Distribution is a rule about syntax, not about intent. A bare type parameter on the checked side splits unions and swallows` never` , and wrapping that parameter in a tuple turns both behaviors off. When a conditional type returns something unexpected, look at the left of` extends` first, then decide whether you want one answer per member or one answer for the whole union. For more type-level patterns, see[Complex Typing in TypeScript](https://blog.openreplay.com/forever-functional-complex-typing-in-typescript/) .


## FAQs


What does a distributive conditional type return when you pass any or unknown?


Passing any to a distributive conditional type returns the union of both branches, so IsString<any> resolves to boolean. The exception is when the type on the right of extends is itself any. The unknown type is not a union and does not split. It is checked as one type and usually takes the false branch, so IsString<unknown> resolves to false.


Does adding a constraint to the type parameter stop distribution?


No. A constraint such as T extends string | number in the parameter list only limits which arguments are allowed. Distribution depends on whether T appears bare on the left of extends inside the conditional. A constrained parameter used bare still splits a union argument member by member. Only wrapping it, for example as \[T\] extends \[U\], switches distribution off.


Does ReturnType distribute over a union of function types?


Yes. ReturnType is defined as a conditional type that checks the bare parameter T against a function signature and uses infer to capture the return type, so it distributes. ReturnType<(() => string) | (() => number)> evaluates each function separately and resolves to string | number. Parameters and InstanceType follow the same pattern and also distribute over union arguments.
